options: SQL Server having results ready to send but waiting because the client hasn't yet consumed the network buffer it already holds
The physical latency of the network cable or switch between client and server
Time spent waiting for a data page to be read from disk
Time spent waiting for a transaction log write to complete
questions.explain: ASYNC_NETWORK_IO reflects the client's consumption rate relative to how fast SQL Server can produce rows, not raw network hardware latency.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a high ASYNC_NETWORK_IO total usually indicate?
options: A problem on the client side — slow row-by-row processing, oversized result sets, or unnecessary data being pulled — rather than a SQL Server performance defect
A definite SQL Server CPU bottleneck
Corrupted data pages requiring DBCC CHECKDB
An undersized transaction log
questions.explain: The lesson frames this wait type as usually pointing at the client's consumption rate, not at anything wrong with SQL Server itself.

questions.q: Which is a classic client-side cause of high ASYNC_NETWORK_IO named in this lesson?
options: Row-by-row client processing that does meaningful work between fetching each row instead of pulling the full result set quickly
Running DBCC SQLPERF to clear wait statistics
Adding a covering index to a frequently queried table
Increasing max server memory
questions.explain: Fetching one row, doing real work (UI updates, API calls, file writes), then fetching the next slows the client's consumption rate and drives up this wait.

questions.q: How can you check whether ASYNC_NETWORK_IO is concentrated on specific applications rather than pervasive across the whole workload?
options: Join session_id from sys.dm_exec_sessions/sys.dm_exec_requests and look at program_name and host_name
Query sys.dm_os_wait_stats a second time with no filter
Run DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR) and see if it disappears
Check sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats for the affected database
questions.explain: program_name and host_name on session/request DMVs identify which specific client applications and hosts are accumulating the wait.

questions.q: ASYNC_NETWORK_IO is the top wait type on a server, concentrated almost entirely on one third-party reporting tool's sessions, with every other application clean. What should you do, per this lesson?
options: Investigate that reporting tool's fetch pattern and result-set size first, and avoid spending time tuning SQL Server's CPU or storage configuration for this
Immediately add more CPU cores to the server
Rebuild every index on every table in the database
Conclude the network switch is failing and replace it
questions.explain: Concentration on a single client application's sessions strongly supports a client-side cause, making SQL Server-side tuning the wrong response.
